Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we will start with a new module on electrochemical equilibrium.

Key details

  • In this module we are going to study about electrode potential and cell potential.
  • We will derive the Nernst equation.
  • Then we discuss the different types of electrodes.
  • We will look at reference electrodes and also talk about concentration cells.
  • And finally, we will discuss about ion selective electrodes.
  • In today's class we will discuss the origin of electrode potential, we will talk about cell potential and we will derive Nernst equation.
  • Electrochemical equilibria deals with electrochemistry, which is a branch of chemistry which deals with the interconversion of chemical energy and electrical energy.
  • In the galvanic cell, we have chemical energy getting converted into electrical energy.
  • It is the energy in a chemical reaction.
  • Now the reaction has to be a spontaneous reaction because we are not going to provide any energy from outside.
  • The chemical energy has to produce electrical energy.
  • And since we are going to produce electrical energy, that is power, there has to be exchange of electrons.
  • Therefore, we have to have detox reaction.
  • Examples of galvanic cell would be in batteries and fuel cells.
  • We convert electrical energy to chemical energy.
  • Electrical energy is provided externally and.
  • We want to get chemical energy, meaning we want to make a chemical reaction happen.
  • We require a non-spontaneous redox reaction in an electrolytic cell.
  • We use such cells in electroplating, electro refining, and many other metallurgical processes.
  • Whenever we do electrochemical studies, the first thing we require is a redox reaction because we are talking of conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical energy, and both require an exchange of electrons.
  • And one thing we should always remember that oxidation and reduction have to happen simultaneously.
  • The second requirement is that of electrodes.
  • These oxidation and reduction reactions have to happen at the anode and cathode respectively.
  • And the third requirement would be electrolytic conductance.
  • The conductance is through the movement of ions.
  • We have to remember that electrons cannot move through the electrolyte.
  • It's only the ions which are going to cause electrolytic conductance.
  • We can also have molten electrolytes.
  • Apart from that.
